title: Explain the JVM internals — the memory areas (heap, stack, metaspace, code cache), how garbage collection works, what the JIT compiler does, and how you analyze thread dumps, heap dumps, and GC logs when troubleshooting a production Java service.
shortTitle: JVM Internals — Memory areas, GC, JIT, thread dump analysis

s1_definition.profdef: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the runtime that executes Java bytecode. It divides memory into distinct regions: the heap holds objects and is managed by the garbage collector; each thread has its own stack holding method frames and local variables; metaspace stores class metadata; and the code cache stores native machine code produced by the Just-In-Time compiler. The garbage collector automatically reclaims memory from objects no longer reachable, the JIT compiler converts frequently executed bytecode into optimized native code at runtime, and tools like jstack, jmap, and JFR let you inspect threads, heap contents, and performance in a live or crashed process.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the JVM as the National Bank of India head office building. The heap is the giant records vault where all customer files (objects) are stored, and a cleanup crew (the garbage collector) regularly throws out files no one references anymore. Each bank teller (thread) has their own small desk (stack) where they keep the paperwork for the one customer they are serving right now. There is a rulebook room (metaspace) that stores the definitions of what a "Savings Account" or "Trade" even is. And there is a fast-lane counter (code cache) where the bank pre-prepares the forms for the transactions people do most often, so they do not have to fill them from scratch every time.
s1_definition.oneliner: The heap stores your objects and the garbage collector cleans it, each thread gets its own stack, metaspace holds the class blueprints, and the JIT compiler turns hot code into fast native machine code.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the runtime that executes Java bytecode. It divides memory into distinct regions: the heap holds objects and is managed by the garbage collector; each thread has its own stack holding method frames and local variables; metaspace stores class metadata; and the code cache stores native machine code produced by the Just-In-Time compiler. The garbage collector automatically reclaims memory from objects no longer reachable, the JIT compiler converts frequently executed bytecode into optimized native code at runtime, and tools like jstack, jmap, and JFR let you inspect threads, heap contents, and performance in a live or crashed process.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the JVM as the National Bank of India head office building. The heap is the giant records vault where all customer files (objects) are stored, and a cleanup crew (the garbage collector) regularly throws out files no one references anymore. Each bank teller (thread) has their own small desk (stack) where they keep the paperwork for the one customer they are serving right now. There is a rulebook room (metaspace) that stores the definitions of what a "Savings Account" or "Trade" even is. And there is a fast-lane counter (code cache) where the bank pre-prepares the forms for the transactions people do most often, so they do not have to fill them from scratch every time.

**One line to remember:** The heap stores your objects and the garbage collector cleans it, each thread gets its own stack, metaspace holds the class blueprints, and the JIT compiler turns hot code into fast native machine code.

sections.s2_technical:
The heap is where every object you create with `new` lives, and it is split into generations because most objects die young. The Young Generation has an Eden space plus two Survivor spaces named S0 and S1. When Eden fills up, a Minor GC runs, copying the still-alive objects into a survivor space and discarding the dead ones. Objects that survive several minor collections are promoted to the Old Generation, which holds long-lived objects. A Major or Full GC cleans the Old Generation and is more expensive because it can pause application threads. For example, a short-lived `BigDecimal fee = price.multiply(qty)` computed inside a method lives in Eden and is collected almost immediately, while a cached `Account` object that stays referenced for hours ends up in the Old Generation.

The stack is per-thread and holds a frame for each method call, containing local variables and the return address. When `transfer()` calls `debit()`, a new frame is pushed; when `debit()` returns, its frame is popped. If recursion goes too deep, you get a `StackOverflowError`. Primitives and references live on the stack, but the objects they point to live on the heap.

Metaspace stores class metadata — the structure of every loaded class. It replaced the old PermGen in Java 8 and grows automatically in native memory, which is why old "PermGen space" errors are gone but a classloader leak can still exhaust metaspace. The code cache stores the native code that the JIT produces.

The JIT compiler is what makes Java fast. The JVM first interprets bytecode, and as it notices "hot" methods that run thousands of times, it compiles them to native code using tiered compilation: the C1 compiler does a quick compile with light optimization, and the C2 compiler does heavy optimization for the hottest methods. Optimizations include method inlining (pasting a small method's body into its caller), escape analysis (if an object never leaves a method, it can be allocated on the stack or eliminated), and dead code elimination. For instance, a tight loop computing settlement fees over millions of trades will be compiled by C2 and run close to native speed.

For troubleshooting, a senior developer reaches for specific tools. `jstack <pid>` prints a thread dump showing every thread's state, which reveals BLOCKED or WAITING threads in a deadlock. `jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>` captures a heap dump you analyze in Eclipse MAT to find memory leaks. GC logs enabled with `-Xlog:gc*` show pause times and collection frequency, which you can view in GCViewer. Java Flight Recorder and async-profiler give low-overhead CPU and allocation profiles. A key production nuance is to always fix the heap in containers using `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` so the JVM respects the container memory limit instead of seeing the whole host.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the end-of-day settlement job loads millions of trades into memory to compute fees and totals. Operations noticed the service occasionally freezes for a few seconds and sometimes crashes with an OutOfMemoryError during month-end. We want a small demo that makes the JVM's behavior visible so we understand what is happening.

Problem 1 — When the settlement job creates millions of short-lived fee objects, Eden fills up repeatedly and Minor GC runs constantly. This is exactly how the Young Generation works: short-lived allocations churn through Eden and are cleaned cheaply, but if we allocate too fast, GC pauses add up.

Problem 2 — When the job holds references to every trade in a growing list for the whole run, those objects get promoted to the Old Generation and never get collected until the job ends. This is exactly how a memory leak forms: objects stay reachable longer than needed, the Old Generation fills, and a Full GC (or eventually an OutOfMemoryError) follows.

Problem 3 — When the service hangs, we need to look inside the running process. This is exactly what a thread dump and heap dump are for: we capture the live state and see which threads are stuck and which objects are eating the heap.

The code will contain an `Account` class, a `Trade` record, a `SettlementProcessor` that computes fees (creating short-lived objects to stress the Young Generation) and optionally retains trades (to stress the Old Generation), and a `JvmInternalsDemo` main class that runs the processing, prints heap usage before and after, and tells you which commands to run to capture dumps.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run with a fixed heap and G1GC + GC logging
java -Xms256m -Xmx512m -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.JvmInternalsDemo

# In another terminal, capture diagnostics (find the pid with jps)
jps                                             # list java pids
jstack <pid>                                    # thread dump
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>  # heap dump

# In a container, respect the memory limit instead of a fixed -Xmx
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:+UseG1GC \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.JvmInternalsDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one account for Rajesh (SAV2001), 500,000 Trade objects each for 100 shares of RELIANCE at Rs.2,450, a fee rate of 0.0005, and a JVM started with a 512 MB maximum heap using G1GC.

Step 1: The demo builds a list of 500,000 Trade objects. These are long-lived for the duration of the run because the list holds them, so they occupy heap and after enough minor collections are promoted toward the Old Generation.

Step 2: `printHeap("Before processing")` reads `Runtime` memory counters and logs how many megabytes of heap are already used holding the trade list.

Step 3: `process(trades, false)` loops over every trade. For each one it computes `t.amount()` and then a `fee` BigDecimal. These fee objects are short-lived — once added into the running total they are no longer referenced, so they become garbage. This rapid creation and discarding is what fills Eden and triggers frequent, cheap Minor GCs.

Step 4: Because `retain` is false, no trades are added to the `retained` list, so nothing extra is promoted to the Old Generation. The total fees accumulate into one BigDecimal that is returned.

Step 5: `printHeap("After processing (no retain)")` logs heap usage again. The used figure may actually be similar or lower afterward because the garbage collector reclaimed the short-lived fee objects. The demo then prints the total fees, the retained count (zero), and the exact jstack and jmap commands to inspect the live process.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  JvmInternalsDemo.main()
    │ build 500,000 Trade objects
    ▼
  Heap allocation
    │
    ├─ Young Generation (Eden + S0 + S1)
    │     │ new Trade(...) and new BigDecimal fee(...)
    │     │ Eden fills → Minor GC → live copied to Survivor
    │     ▼
    │   survived several GCs?
    │     ├─ yes → promote to Old Gen
    │     └─ no  → collected (garbage) cheap
    │
    └─ Old Generation
          │ long-lived trade list references
          │ fills over time → Major/Full GC (expensive pause)
          ▼
        if retain=true forever → OutOfMemoryError

  process(trades, retain=false)
    │ per trade: amount() → fee → add to total  (short-lived → Young Gen churn)
    ▼
  printHeap() reads Runtime.totalMemory - freeMemory
    │
    ▼
  Diagnostics (live process)
    ├─ jstack <pid>  → thread states (RUNNABLE/BLOCKED/WAITING)
    ├─ jmap  <pid>   → heap.hprof → analyze in Eclipse MAT
    └─ -Xlog:gc*     → gc.log → view in GCViewer
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM divides memory into several areas, and understanding them is essential for debugging production issues. The heap is where all objects live and is managed by the garbage collector. It is split into a Young Generation, which has Eden and two Survivor spaces for short-lived objects, and an Old Generation for long-lived objects. A Minor GC cleans the Young Generation and is cheap, while a Major or Full GC cleans the Old Generation and is expensive because it can pause the application. Each thread has its own stack holding method frames and local variables, metaspace holds class metadata and replaced the old PermGen, and the code cache holds native code produced by the Just-In-Time compiler.

In my banking settlement work this mattered directly. Our end-of-day job processed hundreds of thousands of trades, creating a storm of short-lived fee objects that churned through Eden and triggered frequent minor collections. That was fine. The real problem came when we accidentally retained every trade in a growing list, which pushed objects into the Old Generation, filled the heap, and eventually caused an OutOfMemoryError. Understanding the generational model is what let me spot that we were holding references longer than necessary.

The JIT compiler is what makes Java fast in production. The JVM interprets bytecode at first, and when it sees a hot method running thousands of times it compiles it to native code using tiered compilation, where the C1 compiler does a quick optimization and the C2 compiler does heavy optimization including inlining and escape analysis. For a tight fee-calculation loop over millions of trades, this means the code runs close to native speed after warm-up.

When a service misbehaves in production, I reach for specific tools. I take a thread dump with jstack to find threads that are blocked or deadlocked, I capture a heap dump with jmap and open it in Eclipse MAT to find what is leaking memory, and I enable GC logging with the Xlog gc flag and analyze it in GCViewer to see pause times and collection frequency. For deeper profiling I use Java Flight Recorder because it has very low overhead.

For garbage collector choice, G1GC is the default from Java 9 onward and gives predictable pause targets, while ZGC gives sub-millisecond pauses for very large heaps. The single most important production habit I follow is to always control the heap size in containers using the MaxRAMPercentage flag so the JVM respects the container's memory limit rather than seeing the entire host, because getting that wrong is a very common cause of containers being killed for exceeding their memory.
